content: The submission of HIV testing services was analyzed by region, as illustrated in Figure 1. This figure provides examples of HIV testing services reviewed during the 2019 WHO guidelines process. Key characteristics of the case examples included in the annex are detailed in Appendix 1. These characteristics encompass intervention themes, target populations, implementing agencies, countries of implementation, and WHO regions. In Bangkok, Thailand, the Health Department of the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration initiated a large-scale HIV research program in 2017–2018, employing the reach, recruit, test, treat, retain (RRTTR) model. This model targets adolescents aged 14–19 who are sexually active, reside in Bangkok, and are not actively psychotic. The RRTTR approach involves reaching out to adolescents who have not recently been tested for STIs/HIV, recruiting them for testing, engaging them in STI/HIV testing, initiating and maintaining antiretroviral therapy (ART) for those testing positive, and retaining them in care. Participants were recruited through peer-to-peer methods and provided with confidential HIV counseling and testing. Structured intervention sessions were conducted to engage participants, orient them to the study components, and motivate them for peer recruitment and STI/HIV testing. Participants could recruit peers and attend a second session on the same day, which included pre-test counseling, STI/HIV testing, and access to condoms, contraceptives, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and linkage to care. In 2017 and 2018, 1,254 and 1,700 adolescents participated, respectively, with 2% receiving pre-test counseling and testing. Those with preliminary positive results underwent confirmatory testing and post-test counseling, following Bangkok's Health Department guidelines. Participants received compensation and transportation support, and those in the intervention group were provided with patient navigation for six months. In Myanmar, the Asian Harm Reduction Network (AHRN) piloted a community empowerment response to enhance HIV testing services (HTS) for people who inject drugs (PWID) in Kachin State. This region faces significant challenges due to drug use, poverty, and stigma. AHRN operates harm reduction programs funded by international organizations, including the Global Fund and USAID/PEPFAR. In 2018, AHRN launched a community prevention program in Waimaw Township, training local community members to provide health education, prevention training, and referrals for HTS. Mobile community-facilitated HTS teams offered group pre-test education, safer injection counseling, and linkage to care for HIV-positive clients. The pilot program demonstrated increased reach and enrollment in care, with 16% of community-based HIV tests yielding positive results and 65% of those testing positive receiving treatment. In Mozambique, a novel approach targeting men over 15 years old was implemented in Zambézia Province. This initiative aimed to address gender disparities in HIV testing, as only 38% of men had been tested compared to 61% of women. The program, led by Jhpiego and CONFHIC, involved coordination with government health entities, training community lay counselors, and mobilizing local leaders. Mobile testing units reached men in workplaces and social settings, with 51,624 men tested, 8% testing positive, and 80% of those linked to care. The program also identified other health issues, such as STIs and hypertension, and referred men for medical male circumcision. The approach has since expanded to other provinces. In Belgium, the Swab2know project, initiated in 2012, focuses on men who have sex with men (MSM). It combines outreach HIV testing sessions with a home-sampling approach using self-collected oral fluid specimens. Participants create online accounts, receive sampling kits, and send samples to a laboratory. Results are uploaded to a secure website, and participants are notified via email. Reactive results prompt immediate counseling and linkage to care. The project has conducted approximately 1,000 tests annually, with a 1% yield of new HIV diagnoses. Most newly diagnosed individuals are successfully linked to specialized care. In Lesotho, the Maseru Seventh Day Adventist (SDA) Health Center established a men’s clinic in 2017 to attract more men and boys to HIV services. The clinic, staffed exclusively by male nurses and counselors, offers male-friendly, integrated services, including HIV testing, ART initiation, and STI and tuberculosis screening. Flexible hours accommodate men’s schedules, resulting in a significant increase in the number of men accessing HIV testing services, from 744 in 2016 to 2,916 in 2017. Most men testing positive were linked to treatment due to Lesotho’s test-and-treat policy. In India, Project Sahay, led by SAATHII with support from the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO), was rolled out across 23 districts in six states. The program aims to identify vulnerable populations and conduct community-based testing to facilitate early ART initiation.
